lesson.title: Stating the Claim: Writing Hypotheses for a Goodness-of-Fit Test
lesson.summary: H0 for a goodness-of-fit test must give the complete hypothesized proportion for every category, while Ha simply claims that at least one proportion differs, a precise wording that is easy to get subtly wrong.
lesson.body:
Writing hypotheses for a goodness-of-fit test follows the same underlying principles as writing hypotheses in general (recall writing hypotheses): state claims about population parameters, not sample statistics. What makes this case distinctive is that the parameter being tested is not a single number but a whole set of population proportions, one for every category of the categorical variable, and those proportions must together add to 1, since they describe a complete probability distribution over that variable, tying back to probability distribution.

H0 must specify the complete hypothesized distribution: an actual numeric proportion for every single category, not a vague verbal claim. Ha then simply states that the true distribution differs from the hypothesized one in at least one category. Ha is never a claim that every category is wrong, and it never names some specific alternative distribution, because there is no single alternative here, just not this one.

Here is the hypothesis-writing process worked through on a new scenario. A candy company claims that its bags contain 30 percent red candies, 25 percent blue, 25 percent yellow, and 20 percent green. Note these add to 100 percent, a necessary check. A student wants to test whether that claim holds up. The correctly written hypotheses are: H0: p_red equals 0.30, p_blue equals 0.25, p_yellow equals 0.25, p_green equals 0.20 (the company's claimed color distribution is correct), and Ha: at least one of these proportions is not as the company claims.

Two mistakes are worth flagging by name because they show up often. Writing H0 only in words, something like the candy proportions match the company's claim, without ever stating the actual numbers, loses the precision the test needs and makes it impossible to compute expected counts from it. And writing Ha as something like all of the proportions are different from what was claimed overstates what a significant result would actually show. A significant chi-square statistic only tells you that at least one category's true proportion differs from what was hypothesized, not which category or categories, and not that every category is off. Figuring out which categories drove a significant result requires looking more closely at the individual (O minus E) contributions, a follow-up step beyond what the test itself concludes.
